CC1.1: Management establishes expectations for ethical behavior and follows through when conduct falls short.
Standards of conduct, leadership communications, acknowledgements, reports of deviations and documented follow-up.
Assess whether leadership demonstrates the stated standards, personnel and relevant contractors understand them, adherence is evaluated, and deviations are addressed consistently and in time.
CC1.2: The governing body provides independent oversight of the development and performance of internal control.
Oversight charter or responsibilities, member qualifications, meeting records, challenges raised and tracked decisions.
Assess the governing body's independence from management, relevant expertise, oversight responsibilities, information received, and evidence that it challenges and follows up on control matters.
CC1.3: Management establishes structures, reporting lines, authorities and responsibilities that support the organization's objectives.
Organization and reporting structures, delegated authorities, role descriptions and outsourced-provider responsibility records.

Assess whether governance and operating structures cover the scoped system, authorities and reporting lines are clear, responsibilities are assigned and communicated, and outsourced responsibilities remain subject to oversight.
CC1.4: The organization attracts, develops and retains people with the competence needed to achieve its objectives.
Role competency requirements, hiring and training records, performance or competency evaluations and succession plans.

Assess how required competence is defined for control responsibilities, how personnel are selected and developed, whether deficiencies are addressed, and how continuity is maintained for important roles.
CC1.5: The organization holds individuals accountable for their internal-control responsibilities while considering performance pressures.
Assigned control ownership, performance expectations, evaluations, incentive structures and corrective or disciplinary follow-up.
Assess whether accountability is explicit, performance is evaluated against control responsibilities, incentives and pressures are considered, and appropriate corrective action follows failures.
CC2.1: The organization obtains or generates relevant, quality information for the design and operation of internal control.
Information requirements, data-flow and asset inventories, report-quality checks, source records and management reporting.

Assess whether control owners have identified the information they need, relevant internal and external data is captured, information is complete and current enough for its purpose, and important assets, locations and flows are maintained.
CC2.2: The organization communicates objectives and internal-control responsibilities to the people who need them.
Policies, role communications, training or acknowledgements, escalation channels and records of significant internal communications.

Assess whether objectives, responsibilities, changes and escalation routes reach the appropriate personnel in a usable and timely form, including access to leadership or the governing body when needed.
CC2.3: The organization communicates with external parties about matters affecting internal control.
Customer and supplier communications, agreements, system descriptions, responsibility statements and incident or complaint reporting channels.
Assess whether relevant commitments, system boundaries, shared responsibilities, changes and reporting channels are communicated to and received from customers, vendors and other external parties.
CC3.1: The organization states its objectives clearly enough to identify and assess risks to their achievement.
Service commitments, system requirements, scoped objectives, risk tolerances and related approvals.

Assess whether objectives reflect the scoped services and commitments, are specific enough for risk analysis, identify acceptable variation or tolerance where relevant, and provide a basis for allocating resources and designing controls.
CC3.2: The organization identifies and analyzes risks to its objectives and decides how those risks will be managed.
Risk methodology, current risk assessments, threat and vulnerability inputs, risk analyses, owners and response decisions.

Assess whether risks are identified across the relevant organizational and system scope, internal and external factors are considered, significance is analyzed consistently, responsible management participates, and responses and residual-risk decisions are recorded.
CC3.3: The organization considers the potential for fraud when assessing risks to its objectives.
Fraud-risk scenarios, incentive and opportunity analysis, misuse-of-technology considerations and resulting control decisions.

Assess whether the risk process considers fraudulent reporting, loss or misuse of assets, misconduct and technology-enabled abuse, including incentives, pressures, opportunities, attitudes and relevant internal or external actors.
CC3.4: The organization identifies and assesses changes that could significantly affect internal control.
Change-impact assessments, new-service or technology reviews, leadership and vendor change records and triggered risk reassessments.

Assess whether material changes in the external environment, business model, leadership, systems, technology, vendors, threats and vulnerabilities trigger timely evaluation and corresponding updates to risks and controls.
CC4.1: The organization performs appropriate ongoing or separate evaluations to determine whether internal control is present and functioning.
Monitoring plans, control evaluations, internal or independent reviews, evaluator qualifications, results and management conclusions.

Assess whether monitoring covers relevant controls, uses a risk-appropriate mix of ongoing and separate evaluation, is performed by competent and sufficiently objective people, adapts to change, and produces supported conclusions.
CC4.2: The organization evaluates and communicates control deficiencies and monitors corrective action.
Evaluation results, Findings, escalation or governance records, remediation Actions, due dates and validation or closure decisions.

Assess whether deficiencies are evaluated for significance, communicated promptly to responsible owners and appropriate leadership, assigned for correction, tracked to due dates, and independently validated before closure where warranted.
CC5.1: The organization selects and develops control activities that reduce risks to acceptable levels.
Risk-to-control mappings, control descriptions, ownership and approval records, segregation analyses and compensating-control decisions.

Assess whether selected activities address identified risks at the appropriate organizational and process levels, include preventive or detective coverage as needed, and handle incompatible duties or documented alternatives.
CC5.2: The organization establishes general control activities over technology that support its objectives.
Technology dependency analysis, infrastructure and security control standards, access and change controls, maintenance records and exceptions.

Assess which technology processes support control operation, whether general controls cover the relevant infrastructure and software, and whether access, acquisition, development and maintenance activities are designed and operated consistently with the identified risks.
CC5.3: The organization deploys control activities through policies that set expectations and procedures that put them into action.
Approved policies and procedures, assigned responsibilities, dated execution records, exceptions, corrective actions and review history.

Assess whether policies state management's expectations, procedures define who does what and when, competent personnel perform the activities, exceptions lead to corrective action, and the documents are reassessed when conditions change.
CC6.1: The organization implements logical-access security over protected information assets to protect them from security events.
Asset and access-point inventories, architecture reviews, authentication and access configurations, encryption or key controls and exception reviews.

Assess whether protected assets and access paths are identified, logical access is restricted and authenticated, new architectures are reviewed, credentials and external access points are managed, and stronger protections such as segmentation or encryption are selected according to risk.
CC6.2: The organization registers and authorizes users before issuing credentials or access and prevents use of credentials that are no longer authorized.
Identity registration, owner approvals, credential issuance, periodic validity reviews and disablement records for people, systems and software.

Assess whether every credential type is tied to an identified and authorized subject, approvals precede issuance, credential validity is reviewed, and credentials are disabled or removed promptly when no longer valid.
CC6.3: The organization grants, changes and removes access according to roles, responsibilities and system design, considering least privilege and segregation of duties.
Role and entitlement definitions, access requests and approvals, change and termination records, access reviews and segregation analyses.

Assess whether access decisions have authorized owners, privileges match current responsibilities, incompatible access is prevented or addressed, changes and removals occur when needed, and roles and rules are periodically reviewed.
CC6.4: The organization restricts physical access to relevant facilities and protected information assets to authorized personnel.
Physical-access approvals and lists, badge and visitor records, access reviews, revocations and recovered-device records.

Assess whether in-scope locations and assets are identified, physical access is authorized and restricted, changes and removals are timely, devices or badges are recovered, and access remains consistent with current responsibilities.
CC6.5: The organization maintains protection of physical assets until data and software can no longer be read or recovered and are no longer needed.
Asset retirement or transfer procedures, sanitization or destruction records, vendor attestations and disposal verification.

Assess whether assets leaving service or control are identified, retention needs are resolved, data and software are rendered inaccessible using an appropriate method, and protection is not removed before sanitization or destruction is verified.
CC6.6: The organization protects against threats from outside its system boundaries through logical-access security measures.
Boundary diagrams, approved channel and port rules, remote-access and authentication settings, firewall or detection configurations and exception records.

Assess whether external access points and permitted activities are defined, credentials are protected in transit, remote access uses risk-appropriate authentication, boundary protections are maintained, and exceptions are authorized and monitored.
CC6.7: The organization restricts information transmission, movement and removal to authorized users and processes and protects the information in transit or removal.
Transfer authorizations, data-loss prevention rules, secure-channel or encryption settings, removable-media controls, endpoint protections and exception records.

Assess whether sensitive transfers and removals are identified and authorized, channels and media provide protection appropriate to risk, endpoints are covered, and attempted or exceptional transfers are detected and followed up.
CC6.8: The organization prevents or detects and acts on unauthorized or malicious software.
Software-installation restrictions, change-detection records, change approvals, anti-malware coverage and alerts, scan results and response records.

Assess whether software installation and modification are restricted, unauthorized changes can be detected, approved change processes are used, relevant servers and endpoints are protected, and detections or externally received assets are handled before exposure.
CC7.1: The organization detects configuration changes that introduce vulnerabilities and exposure to newly discovered vulnerabilities.
Configuration standards and compliance results, change-detection alerts, component inventories, vulnerability scans, remediation records and approved exceptions.

Assess whether standards cover the scoped infrastructure and software, deviations and unknown components are detected, vulnerability monitoring includes new disclosures and significant changes, and identified weaknesses are prioritized and resolved in time.
CC7.2: The organization monitors system components and operations for anomalies and analyzes whether they are security events.
Monitoring coverage, logging and alert configurations, threat inputs, anomaly triage records, tool-health checks and resulting event records.

Assess whether monitoring addresses malicious activity, natural events and errors across the scoped system, relevant anomalies are collected and filtered, qualified personnel analyze them promptly, and detection tools themselves are monitored for effective operation.
CC7.3: The organization evaluates security events to determine whether they are incidents and acts to prevent or address failures of its objectives.
Event criteria, triage and impact analyses, escalation decisions, incident records and resulting preventive or corrective actions.

Assess whether detected events reach responsible personnel, consistent criteria distinguish events from incidents, system and confidentiality impacts are evaluated where relevant, and decisions and actions are documented and reviewed.
CC7.4: The organization executes a defined incident-response program to understand, contain, remediate and communicate identified incidents.
Incident-response roles and procedures, timelines, containment and remediation records, communications, exercises and effectiveness reviews.

Assess whether roles and external resources are assigned, incidents are understood and prioritized, containment and remediation are executed, interim operations and communications are managed, and exercises or incident trends drive program improvement.
CC7.5: The organization identifies, develops and implements activities to recover from identified security incidents.
Recovery plans and tests, restoration and validation records, root-cause analysis, lessons learned, control changes and communications.

Assess whether recovery restores affected environments in a controlled manner, validates functionality, addresses root cause and recurrence, communicates needed information, and tests plausible scenarios with resulting plan or control improvements.
CC8.1: The organization controls changes to infrastructure, data, software and procedures through authorization, design, documentation, testing, approval and implementation.
Change requests, impact and security reviews, approvals, test results, release records, emergency changes, patch records and post-change validation.

Assess whether ordinary and emergency changes are controlled across their life cycle, objectives and security impacts are evaluated, responsibilities are segregated where appropriate, changes are tracked and tested before release, and unauthorized or unsuccessful changes are detected and addressed.
CC9.1: The organization selects and develops activities to mitigate risks arising from potential business disruptions.
Business-disruption risk assessments, continuity and communication procedures, alternate-processing arrangements, exercise results and risk-treatment decisions.

Assess whether credible disruption scenarios are identified, mitigation and recovery arrangements align with system commitments, responsibilities and communications are defined, alternatives are workable, and relevant financial-risk treatment such as insurance is considered without substituting for operational controls.
CC9.2: The organization assesses and manages risks associated with vendors and business partners.
Vendor inventory and tiering, due diligence, agreements and requirements, assurance reviews, issue tracking, monitoring and termination records.

Assess whether relevant third parties and downstream dependencies are identified and risk-tiered, requirements and responsibilities are established, risk is evaluated before and during use, issues and service changes are tracked, and termination addresses access and information return or removal. For confidentiality scope, assess relevant confidentiality commitments and oversight.
A1.1: The organization maintains, monitors and evaluates processing capacity and system-component use so it can respond to capacity demand.
Current and peak utilization measures, baselines, forecasts, capacity tolerances, resilience assumptions and resulting change decisions.

Assess whether current use is measured, expected average and peak demand is forecast, component failure and resilience assumptions are considered, thresholds align with availability objectives, and forecasted constraints trigger timely capacity changes.
A1.2: The organization implements and monitors environmental protections, backup processes and recovery infrastructure needed to support availability objectives.
Environmental risk and alert records, protection maintenance, backup scope and job results, failure follow-up, storage design, failover records and recoverability analyses.

Assess whether relevant environmental and recoverability threats are identified, protections and alerts operate, required data is backed up and failures are corrected, backup separation is appropriate, and alternate infrastructure or failover arrangements support the stated availability objectives.
A1.3: The organization tests recovery-plan procedures that support system recovery.
Approved test scenarios, participant and dependency scope, recovery and backup-integrity results, gaps, remediation Actions and retest records.

Assess whether tests reflect plausible threats and the scoped system, include important components, vendors and personnel dependencies, verify backup integrity and completeness, document recovery results against objectives, and lead to tracked plan or system improvements.
C1.1: The organization identifies and maintains confidential information according to its confidentiality objectives.
Confidentiality definitions and inventories, classification or designation records, retention rules, legal or contractual requirements and protection from premature destruction.

Assess whether confidential information is defined and identified when received or created, applicable commitments and retention needs are recorded, information is retained no longer than necessary unless required, and it is protected from destruction during the approved retention period.
C1.2: The organization disposes of confidential information according to its confidentiality objectives.
Retention schedules, destruction eligibility records, approved erasure or destruction results, provider confirmations and exception follow-up.

Assess whether confidential information is identified when retention ends, disposal covers relevant systems, media and service providers, approved methods make the information unavailable as intended, and failures or exceptions are tracked to resolution.
PI1.1: Define the information and processing specifications needed for the system to produce its intended results.
Processing specifications, data definitions and agreed requirements.
PI1.2: Accept inputs that meet the system's quality and authorization needs.
Input validation rules, authorization records and rejected-input handling.
PI1.3: Carry out processing as intended and identify or resolve processing errors.
Processing controls, reconciliation records and exception resolution.
PI1.4: Produce and deliver outputs that meet the system's processing requirements.
Output checks, delivery records and exception follow-up.
PI1.5: Protect stored inputs, processing data and outputs so processing integrity can be maintained.
Storage controls, retention settings and integrity verification records.
P1.1: Communicate the organization's relevant personal-information practices and purposes to the affected people.
Privacy notices, publication/version records and applicable delivery evidence.
P2.1: Explain relevant choices and consent options for personal-information processing.
Choice/consent notices, interfaces and communication records.
P3.1: Collect personal information in line with the stated purposes and applicable commitments.
Collection forms, purpose/data maps and collection controls.
P3.2: Obtain and retain explicit consent where the organization's collection practices require it.
Consent mechanism, recorded decisions and withdrawal handling.
P4.1: Use personal information consistently with the purposes and commitments governing it.
Purpose-to-use mapping, access restrictions and use reviews.
P4.2: Retain personal information according to the purposes and commitments that justify keeping it.
Retention rules, assigned owners and retention execution records.
P4.3: Dispose of personal information through appropriate secure handling when retention ends.
Disposal procedures, execution records and verification.
P5.1: Provide appropriate access to personal information after verifying the requesting person's identity.
Subject-request procedure, identity checks and response records.
P5.2: Handle requests to correct or amend personal information through an established process.
Correction requests, decisions, changes and response records.
P6.1: Disclose personal information consistently with the relevant consent and stated purposes.
Disclosure rules, consent context and approved disclosure records.
P6.2: Retain records that explain authorized disclosures of personal information.
Disclosure logs, recipient information and authorization context.
P6.3: Record and address unauthorized disclosures rather than treating them as ordinary data sharing.
Disclosure incident records, investigation and corrective follow-up.
P6.4: Address privacy responsibilities when third parties receive personal information.
Third-party commitments, agreements and oversight records.
P6.5: Establish how third parties communicate relevant personal-information disclosure issues.
Contractual notification responsibilities and received notification records.
P6.6: Maintain a process for evaluating and carrying out applicable breach notifications.
Breach assessment, notification decisions and communication records.
P6.7: Support applicable disclosure-accounting requests with appropriate records and responses.
Request handling, disclosure accounting and response records.
P7.1: Maintain personal information with the quality needed for its intended purposes.
Data quality checks, correction records and ownership decisions.
P8.1: Handle privacy complaints and monitor whether privacy practices follow the organization's commitments.
Complaint records, privacy reviews and corrective follow-up.

groups.CC1: Typical management controls assign governance responsibilities and demonstrate how expectations are communicated, applied and followed up. Distinguish the control's design from evidence that people actually performed it.
groups.CC2: Typical management controls identify who needs information, its source and the communication channel. Retain evidence that useful information reached the intended audience.
groups.CC3: Typical management controls define risk-assessment responsibilities and triggers, record decisions and connect identified risks to responses.
groups.CC4: Typical management controls evaluate operation, identify deficiencies and track corrective decisions through validation.
groups.CC5: Typical management controls explain who performs the activity, its scope, trigger or frequency and how exceptions are handled. A policy alone does not demonstrate operation.
groups.CC6: Typical management controls cover the relevant access paths and information lifecycle. Check enforcement, authorization records and exceptions in the actual system boundary.
groups.CC7: Typical management controls connect detection to evaluation, response and recovery. Retain dated records showing actions and decisions during the observation period.
groups.CC8: Typical management controls establish change responsibility, review, testing and release handling. Check ordinary and emergency paths and any exceptions.
groups.CC9: Typical management controls connect disruption or third-party risks to resilience decisions, agreements and ongoing follow-up.
groups.A1: Typical management controls connect availability commitments to capacity, resilience and recovery arrangements and retain operating and test results.
groups.C1: Typical management controls identify confidential information, its handling rules and lifecycle responsibilities, including disposal.
groups.PI1: Typical management controls define expected processing, validate inputs and outputs and track exceptions to resolution within the system boundary.
groups.privacy: Typical management controls connect the stated privacy practice to accountable owners, request or event handling and appropriately protected records. Use minimized examples rather than unnecessary personal information.
